#### July Temperature

[![Image 6: July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202607.png) July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202607.png "July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/1/7/1895-2026) over the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) in July was 76.89°F, 3.30°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking as the warmest July](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202607#1) in the 132-year record. The average temperature was 0.12°F warmer than July 1936 (76.77°F) and 0.16°F warmer than July 2012 (76.73°F). It was also the warmest monthly average temperature recorded for the CONUS (1895–2026) and concluded the [warmest 12-month period](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/12/0/1895-2026) in the record (August 2025–July 2026).

Above-average temperatures extended across the entire CONUS, with much-above-average temperatures observed throughout much of the interior West, Southwest, Rockies, northern Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as parts of the Gulf Coast and Southeast. All CONUS states ranked among the warmest third of their record and were at least 1°F above their 20th-century average, with 13 states ranking among their five warmest Julys. [Wyoming](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/48/tavg/1/7/1895-2026) recorded its warmest July and warmest month on record, with temperatures 6.3°F above average and 0.9°F warmer than its previous July record set in 2007.

The CONUS [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/1/7/1895-2026) in July was 89.5°F, 2.9°F above average, [ranking as the sixth-warmest month](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmax/202607#1) on record for average high temperatures. Maximum temperatures were particularly high across portions of the interior West, northern tier and Florida Peninsula, while near- or below-average temperatures were observed across parts of the southern Plains and Midwest. According to [NOAA's nClimGrid-Daily dataset](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/nclimgrid-daily), 98 counties had their highest county-average daily maximum temperature in the 76-year period of record (1951–2026), representing 6.7% of the CONUS area and an estimated population of 6.1 million people (based on 2020 U.S. Census data).

The CONUS [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/1/7/1895-2026) was 64.2°F, 3.7°F above average, [ranking as the warmest month](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmin/202607#1) on record for average low temperatures, surpassing July 2022 by 0.7°F. Elevated overnight temperatures were exceptionally widespread, with above-average minimums spanning nearly the entire CONUS and pockets of record warmth observed across parts of the West, Rockies, Upper Midwest, Deep South and Southeast.

Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jul/1-month), the CONUS temperature-related energy demand during July was 201% of average and the eighth-highest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### July Precipitation

[![Image 16: July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202607.png) July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202607.png "July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The [total precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) averaged across the CONUS in July was 2.55 inches, 0.23 inch below the 20th-century average, ranking in the [driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202607#1) of the 132-year record and the driest July since 2012.

Precipitation across the CONUS during July reflected a mix of wet and dry conditions. Below-average precipitation occurred across portions of the northern tier, including parts of the northern Rockies, northern Plains, Upper Midwest and Northeast, as well as parts of the southern Plains, Mississippi Valley, central Gulf and Southeast. In contrast, pockets of above-average precipitation were observed across parts of the West and Southwest, central Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as portions of Texas, the Tennessee and lower Ohio valleys, Mid-Atlantic and lower Northeast.

The regional precipitation contrasts were particularly evident across the Northeast. Statewide, [Maine](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/17/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) had its fourth-driest July on record (46% below average), while [Connecticut](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/6/pcp/1/7/1895-2026), [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) and [Massachusetts](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/19/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) recorded their sixth-, seventh- and 12th-wettest July on record, respectively, with precipitation 72% to 105% above average.

[Precipitation across Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/1/7/1925-2026) in July averaged 4.30 inches, 1.02 inches above the 1925–2000 average, [ranking in the wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/50/pcp/202607#1) of the 102-year record. Southern and southwestern portions of the state, including the Alaska Peninsula, received above-average to much-above-average precipitation, with Anchorage tying its highest July precipitation total on record. In contrast, portions of the Alaska Panhandle received below-average precipitation.

[Precipitation across Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) in July averaged 5.20 inches, 0.56 inch above the 1991–2020 average, [ranking in the wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/51/pcp/202607#1) of the 36-year record. Despite the above-average statewide precipitation, localized dry conditions occurred across parts of the islands, with Honolulu receiving just 0.02 inch of rainfall, tying its driest July on record.

#### Drought

According to the August 4 [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx), about 48.5% of the CONUS was in drought, an increase of about 0.7 percentage points since the end of June. Drought persisted over much of the interior West, Southwest and Rockies, and expanded or intensified across parts of the Northwest, southern and northern Plains, Upper Midwest and far Northeast. In contrast, drought contracted or decreased in intensity across portions of the Lower Mississippi Valley, Tennessee Valley and much of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic region. In Puerto Rico, more than two-thirds of the island was in drought, with more than one-third classified as severe drought or worse.

See the accompanying national [Drought Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/drought/202607) for further details.

#### Other Notable Events

Several notable events in July included:

*   **Northern Rockies and West:** A heat wave on July 12 brought all-time record high temperatures to multiple airport stations across Idaho, Utah, Wyoming and Montana, including Idaho Falls, ID (103°F), Salt Lake City, UT (109°F), Sheridan, WY (109°F), Billings, MT (111°F) and Miles City, MT (115°F).
*   **Wyoming:** Boysen Dam recorded a monthly average temperature of 81.3°F in July, setting an all-time record for the highest monthly average temperature observed at any weather station in Wyoming history. _See the High Plains RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Oregon:** Wildfires across eastern Oregon burned more than 140,000 acres in July, triggering local evacuations and regional air quality hazards.
*   **Southwest:** Elevated overnight temperatures in late July set an all-time record warm low temperature of 99°F in Laughlin, Nevada, and tied record warm low temperatures in Phoenix, Arizona (97°F), and Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada (96°F).
*   **Nebraska and South Dakota:** A late-July heat wave featuring heat index values above 120°F and light winds led to an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 cattle fatalities across Nebraska and South Dakota. _See the High Plains RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Iowa:** Back-to-back heavy rainfall events during July 2–4 dropped 5 to 10 inches of rain across central Iowa, causing major flash flooding in Polk, Story and Jasper counties and driving Fourmile Creek near Des Moines to its second-highest crest on record. _See the [NWS Des Moines, IA summary](https://www.weather.gov/dmx/July\_2\_4\_2026\_Flash\_Flooding) and Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Michigan:** A high-instability squall line on July 3 swept across Lower Michigan with wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph, causing tree damage and knocking out electrical power to nearly 400,000 utility customers in the Detroit metro area. _See the [NWS Detroit, MI summary](https://www.weather.gov/dtx/severeweather070326) for additional details._
*   **Missouri:** On July 4, a line of severe thunderstorms produced estimated straight-line wind gusts up to 105 mph east of Jefferson City to Osage City along the Missouri River corridor, causing structural and tree damage across Cole, Callaway and Osage counties. _See the [NWS St. Louis, MO summary](https://www.weather.gov/lsx/7\_4\_26) for additional details._
*   **Illinois, Kentucky and Missouri:** Training thunderstorms during July 9–11 produced a broad swath of 6 to 11 inches of rainfall across southern Illinois, western Kentucky and southeastern Missouri, triggering flash flooding and washed-out roadways. _See the [NWS Paducah, KY summary](https://www.weather.gov/pah/July9-11\_2026\_Flooding\_Severe) and Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Upper Midwest:** Canadian wildfire smoke transported into the central U.S. during mid-July produced Minnesota's worst air quality outbreak in at least 50 years. _See the Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Wisconsin and Illinois:** An outbreak of severe weather on July 27 produced an EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 140 mph that tracked through Fox Crossing and Menasha in the Appleton, Wisconsin area, injuring at least 60 people before moving over Lake Winnebago as a waterspout. The storm system also produced seven tornadoes and 80 to 100 mph straight-line wind gusts across the Chicago metro area. _See the [NWS Green Bay, WI summary](https://www.weather.gov/grb/07272026\_SevereStorms), [NWS Chicago, IL summary](https://www.weather.gov/lot/2026\_07\_27\_severe\_flood) and the accompanying [Tornadoes Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202607) for additional details._
*   **Texas Hill Country:** Persistent, heavy rainfall during July 13–17 dropped up to 28.23 inches of rain near Knippa, Texas, triggering major flash flooding across multiple river basins. The [Nueces River below Uvalde](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/flood_UVLT2_20260714-20260719.png) reached a record major flood crest of 28.01 feet on July 16, breaking its 1996 record of 24.88 feet. _See the preliminary [WPC Storm Summary](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/storm\_summaries/storm11/stormsum\_6.html) and the Southern RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Galveston, Texas:** On July 31, Galveston Scholes Field reached 100°F, marking its first triple-digit temperature ever recorded during the month of July in over a century of observations. _See the Southern RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Carolinas, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast:** Numerous locations observed their warmest July 4 on record during an early-July heat wave stretching from Highlands, NC, to Cape Cod, MA. Daily maximum temperature records included Raleigh, NC (103°F), Washington, D.C. (103°F), Danville, VA (103°F) and Richmond, VA (100°F). Atlantic City, NJ, reached 106°F during the early-July heat wave, tying its all-time highest temperature on record. _See the Northeast RCC Report and Southeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **West Virginia:** A severe storm outbreak on July 21 produced nine tornadoes across West Virginia—one of the state's most active tornado days since 1950—and 4 to 8 inches of rainfall, triggering a Flash Flood Emergency in Upshur County where Sand Run at Buckhannon reached its highest river crest on record. _See the Northeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **North Carolina:** Raleigh-Durham International Airport recorded 12.16 inches of rain in July (its second-wettest July on record), receiving more precipitation in a single month than during the entire January–June period combined (11.88 inches) and alleviating severe drought along the I-85/40 corridor. _See the Southeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Northeast and Mid-Atlantic:** Slow-moving thunderstorms on July 28–29 produced widespread flash flooding from eastern Pennsylvania to southern New England. Storm total rainfall reached nearly 12 inches in eastern New York, with 1,000-year rainfall recurrence intervals observed in Schodack (11.80 in) and Kinderhook (11.48 in). Albany, NY (5.45 in) and Worcester, MA (4.56 in) each set all-time daily rainfall records for the month of July on July 29. _See the [NWS Binghamton, NY summary](https://www.weather.gov/bgm/pastRainfallJuly29\_August032026) and Northeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Alaska:** Cool and wet conditions prevailed across much of southern Alaska, with Talkeetna recording its wettest July since 1922 (10.59 in) and Anchorage tying 2001 for its wettest July on record (4.49 in). Cold Bay recorded an 85-year monthly record low temperature of 32°F on July 6. Additionally, end-of-July sea ice extent in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas was the highest since 2000 and 2003, respectively. _See the Western RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Hawaiʻi:** Unseasonably dry conditions prevailed across parts of the islands during July, with Honolulu receiving just 0.02 inch of rainfall, tying its driest July on record. _See the Western RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Puerto Rico:** San Juan recorded its driest July in 128 years of observations with just 0.54 inch of rain, breaking the previous record of 1.10 inches set in 1929. According to the August 4 U.S. Drought Monitor, more than two-thirds of Puerto Rico was in drought, with more than one-third of the island classified as severe drought or worse. _See the Southeast RCC Report for additional details._

#### January–July Temperature

[![Image 22: January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202607.png) January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202607.png "January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/ytd/7/1895-2026) for the CONUS during January–July was 55.5°F, 4.2°F above the 20th-century average. The period [ranked second warmest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202607#7) in the 132-year record, 0.17°F cooler than January–July 2012. Most of the CONUS saw above- to much-above-average temperatures, with 30 states ranking among their 10 warmest January–July periods on record. Eight states recorded their warmest January–July period on record.

Based on the [NOAA climate regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/mapping/-1/tavg/202607/ytd/rank), the West and Southwest each experienced their warmest January–July period on record, while the South ranked second warmest, the Northern Rockies and Plains third warmest and the Northwest region fourth warmest. The [Southwest region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/time-series/107/tavg/7/7/1895-2026) was especially anomalous, averaging 6.0°F above its 20th-century January–July baseline and eclipsing the previous record, tied in 2000 and 2018, by 2.1°F.

At the county level, [more than 450 counties](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/county/mapping/110/tavg/202607/ytd/rank)—covering over one-quarter of the CONUS and affecting an estimated 72 million people—recorded their warmest January–July on record, reflecting the broad geographic footprint of the period's record warmth.

The CONUS average [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/ytd/7/1895-2026) was 67.9°F, 4.7°F above average, and the average [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/ytd/7/1895-2026) was 43.0°F, 3.8°F above average, with both measures ranking second warmest on record. Averaged over the entire [Rockies and Westward region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/reference-maps/rockies-and-westward), the January–July period set new records, with an average maximum temperature 0.7°F above the 1934 Dust Bowl-era record and an average minimum temperature 0.6°F above the 2015 record.

Based on [REDTI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jul/year-to-date), the temperature-related energy demand for CONUS from January through July was 37% of average and the 10th-lowest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### January–July Precipitation

[![Image 32: January–July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202607.png) January–July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202607.png "January–July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The average [precipitation total](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) across the CONUS during January–July was 16.28 inches, 1.80 inches below the 20th-century average, [ranking in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202607#7) of the 132-year record and the driest January–July since 2012.

Much of the western half of the CONUS received below- to much-below-average precipitation during January–July, along with parts of the Lower Mississippi and Tennessee valleys, Southeast, Mid-Atlantic and coastal areas of the Northeast. In contrast, portions of the Midwest and Great Lakes received above-average precipitation. These regional differences were reflected in statewide rankings; for example, [South Carolina](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/38/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) (67.1% of average) ranked third driest while [Michigan](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/20/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) (131.9% of average) ranked third wettest.

Among select locations with long-term station records, [Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/haywood/prcp/Jan-Jul.prcp.GreenBay.png) (1887–2026), recorded its highest January–July precipitation [total of 27.65 inches](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/city/time-series/USW00014898/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026), 9.02 inches (nearly 50%) above the 1991–2020 average. In contrast, [Savannah, Georgia](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/haywood/prcp/Jan-Jul.prcp.Savannah.png) (1948–2026), recorded its lowest January–July precipitation [total of 14.89 inches](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/city/time-series/USW00003822/pcp/ytd/7/1948-2026), just over half of its 1991–2020 average of 29.00 inches.

In Alaska, [year-to-date precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/ytd/7/1925-2026) totaled 18.71 inches, 1.80 inches above the 1925–2000 average, ranking in the wettest third of the 102-year record. Above-average precipitation was observed across much of the Alaska mainland, while portions of the Aleutians and parts of the Panhandle received below-average precipitation.

In Hawaiʻi, [year-to-date precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) totaled 59.82 inches, 25.43 inches above the 1991–2020 average (173.9% of average), ranking as the [wettest January–July](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/haywood/51/pcp/12) in the 36-year record.

#### Extremes

The year-to-date [USCEI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/) was 137% above the long-term average, ranking as the second-highest January–July value in the 117-year record. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/1) spanned 78% of the CONUS, the second-largest extent on record, while warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/2) covered 73% of the CONUS, the third-largest extent on record. [Dry extremes](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/3), as measured by low Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) values, covered 45% of the CONUS, ranking as the second-largest January–July extent on record, behind 1934 during the Dust Bowl era.

[Regionally](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/cei-hi), the Southwest and South set their highest January–July CEI values on record, while the West ranked second highest and the Ohio Valley fourth highest for the period. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/1-hi) broke several January–July records, covering the entire West and Southwest regions (100%), along with 92% of the South (record high) and 97% of the Northwest (fourth highest). Warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/2-hi) were also widespread, covering more than 98% of the West, Southwest and South, each a record high for the period, and 93% of the Northwest (third highest). The spatial extent of [very low PDSI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/3-lo) values set January–July records in the Southwest (96%) and Southeast (67%), and was much above average across the West, Northwest, South, Ohio Valley and Northeast (second highest). In contrast, extreme 1-day precipitation totals set a January–July record in the [Ohio Valley](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/ce/ytd/4), covering 39% of the region.

#### Monthly Outlook

Above-average August [temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdotempoutlook-202607.gif) are favored across the central and southern tiers of the CONUS, with portions of coastal California and the southern Plains having a greater than 50% likelihood of above-average temperatures. [Precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdoprcpoutlook-202607.gif) has equal chances of being above or below average across much of the CONUS, except in parts of the interior West and Southwest where above-average rainfall is favored and in portions of the southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley where below-average precipitation is favored. Visit the Climate Prediction Center's [Official 30-Day Forecasts](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/30day/) for more details.

[Drought](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdodroughtoutlook-202607.png) is expected to persist and expand across parts of the Northwest and east of the Rockies, including portions of the Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Drought conditions are expected to improve across parts of the interior West and Southwest, and along much of the eastern seaboard. Visit the [U.S. Monthly Drought Outlook](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/expert_assessment/mdo_summary.php) website for more details.

Significant wildland [fire potential for August](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/nifcfireoutlook-202607.png) is above normal across the Northwest, Great Basin and central Rockies, parts of the northern and southern Plains, the Lower Mississippi Valley, southern Florida and Puerto Rico. For additional information on wildland fire potential, visit the [National Interagency Fire Center](https://www.nifc.gov/) website.

#### Northeast _(Information provided by the [Northeast Regional Climate Center](http://www.nrcc.cornell.edu/))_

July in the Northeast featured a record-setting heat wave, locally extreme rainfall, and several significant severe weather events.

**Read the full Northeast RCC report...**
##### **Temperature**

The average temperature for July in the Northeast was 71.1°F, 0.9°F hotter than normal. July average temperatures for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 0.4°F below normal in Connecticut to 1.8°F above normal in West Virginia, with nine of the states being warmer than normal. This July ranked as the 14th hottest July since recordkeeping began in 1895 for Delaware and as the 17th hottest on record for Maryland and West Virginia. A heat wave in early July set or tied multiple records. Atlantic City, New Jersey, tied its all-time hottest temperature of 106°F, while Wilmington, Delaware, tied its hottest July temperature of 103°F. Low temperatures of 84°F at Washington, D.C.; 80°F at Providence, Rhode Island; and 71°F at Caribou, Maine, tied as each site's all-time hottest low temperatures on record. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and Dulles Airport, Virginia, tied their hottest low temperatures for July at 81°F and 78°F, respectively. Several other notable records were set/tied including longest streak of days with a high of 100°F or higher. See the Notable Weather Events section below for more information. On July 16, Dulles Airport, Virginia, had a low of 81°F: its first time on record with a low of at least 80°F, the hottest low temperature for July beating the record set earlier in the month, and its hottest low temperature for any month on record.

##### **Precipitation**

During July, the Northeast received 4.53 inches of precipitation, which was 104% of normal. Precipitation during July for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 51% of normal in Maine to 198% of normal in Rhode Island, with eight states being wetter than normal. This July was the fourth-driest July for Maine but ranked among the 20 wettest for five other states: Connecticut, sixth wettest; Rhode Island, seventh wettest; Massachusetts, 12th wettest; Delaware, 15th wettest; and New Jersey, 18th wettest. On July 29, Albany, New York, had 5.45 inches of rain and Worcester, Massachusetts, saw 4.56 inches of rain, qualifying as each site's wettest July day on record.

##### **Drought**

The U.S. Drought Monitor from July 7 showed 25% of the Northeast in drought and 12% of the region as abnormally dry. Extreme drought was present in portions of Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey, while severe and/or moderate drought were found in locations closer to the coast along a path from Maryland to Maine, as well as some southern locations like southern and eastern West Virginia. During July, drought contracted in areas that saw ample rainfall and recovering streamflow, groundwater levels and soil moisture. For example, extreme drought was erased from much of Maryland and New Jersey, while severe drought in West Virginia, New York, and Rhode Island was reduced to small patches. The notable exception was Maine, where moderate drought spread due to reduced rainfall and declining streamflow, groundwater levels, and soil moisture. The U.S. Drought Monitor from July 28 showed 21% of the Northeast in drought and 18% of the region as abnormally dry. Drought conditions continued to have impacts in the region. At times during July, USGS 7-day streamflow was record low in places like the Delmarva Peninsula, southeastern Pennsylvania, coastal New Jersey, central New York, and central Maine. Groundwater levels were record low at times during the month in several areas including parts of Maryland, southeastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, eastern New York, and southeastern Massachusetts. Water conservation continued to be encouraged in some areas, with a few water suppliers in parts of southern New Hampshire, southern New England, southeastern New York, northeastern New Jersey, and south-central Pennsylvania having mandatory water restrictions or watering bans. In early July, a report from southwestern West Virginia noted that people continued to fill water tanks at the municipal water source. Baltimore, Maryland, officials tested their backup water system for the first time in 20 years. Drought and hot temperatures contributed to a fishkill in the Potomac River in Maryland. Condition monitoring reports from West Virginia during the month noted that hot, dry weather slowed crop and pasture growth and left fields dry, second cutting of hay yields were reduced (in some locations by over 50%) compared to an average year, and that a grower opted to have cattle graze a hay field instead of cutting it due to drought. Additionally, some corn crops in Delaware were a loss.

##### **Notable Weather**

From July 1–5, the Northeast experienced a record-setting heat wave. For the first time on record, Atlantic City, New Jersey, had three straight days with a high of at least 103°F, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, had three consecutive days with a high of at least 101°F. Atlantic City and Philadelphia had their greatest number of days with a high of at least 103°F and at least 101°F, respectively, for any month on record. It became the only July on record to have three consecutive days with a high of at least 102°F in Wilmington, Delaware. Several sites including Kennedy Airport, New York; Harrisburg, Pennsylvania; and Boston, Massachusetts, had their longest streak of days with a high of at least 100°F. Both Atlantic City and Kennedy Airport set/tied their record for greatest number of days with a high of at least 100°F for any month on record with 4 days and 3 days, respectively. Similarly, Wilmington and LaGuardia Airport, New York, set/tied their record for greatest number of days with a high of at least 100°F for July, with 3 days and 2 days, respectively. For the first time in July, Providence, Rhode Island, had a low of at least 80°F, which also tied as its greatest number of such days for any month on record. Portland, Maine, had back-to-back days with a low of at least 72°F, tying its longest such streak. Preliminary data indicated that PJM Interconnection, a power grid operator that services over 65 million customers and covers much of the Mid-Atlantic, set a record for its highest peak load on July 2. The heat caused several Fourth of July events to be cancelled and was linked to at least 39 deaths and hundreds of people seeking heat-related medical care.

There were several other significant events in July. A preliminary total of 37 tornadoes were reported in the Northeast. This included 14 tornadoes in Pennsylvania, well above the state's July average of three tornadoes (based on data from 2001–2025). West Virginia had nine tornadoes compared to its July average of zero, while Maryland had six tornadoes compared to its July average of one. New York had five tornadoes, while New Jersey had four, compared to their July averages of three tornadoes and one tornado, respectively. Preliminary data indicated a few counties including Morris County in New Jersey, Broome County in New York, Pendleton and Pleasants Counties in West Virginia, and Anne Arundel and Talbot Counties in Maryland set or tied their record for greatest number of tornadoes for any month and/or year, with records back to 1950. During the month, there were hundreds of instances of wind damage across the region, along with some large hail.

 A few of the severe weather, flash flood, and other significant events are highlighted below.

#### July Temperature

[![Image 6: July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202607.png) July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202607.png "July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/1/7/1895-2026) over the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) in July was 76.89°F, 3.30°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking as the warmest July](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202607#1) in the 132-year record. The average temperature was 0.12°F warmer than July 1936 (76.77°F) and 0.16°F warmer than July 2012 (76.73°F). It was also the warmest monthly average temperature recorded for the CONUS (1895–2026) and concluded the [warmest 12-month period](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/12/0/1895-2026) in the record (August 2025–July 2026).

Above-average temperatures extended across the entire CONUS, with much-above-average temperatures observed throughout much of the interior West, Southwest, Rockies, northern Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as parts of the Gulf Coast and Southeast. All CONUS states ranked among the warmest third of their record and were at least 1°F above their 20th-century average, with 13 states ranking among their five warmest Julys. [Wyoming](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/48/tavg/1/7/1895-2026) recorded its warmest July and warmest month on record, with temperatures 6.3°F above average and 0.9°F warmer than its previous July record set in 2007.

The CONUS [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/1/7/1895-2026) in July was 89.5°F, 2.9°F above average, [ranking as the sixth-warmest month](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmax/202607#1) on record for average high temperatures. Maximum temperatures were particularly high across portions of the interior West, northern tier and Florida Peninsula, while near- or below-average temperatures were observed across parts of the southern Plains and Midwest. According to [NOAA's nClimGrid-Daily dataset](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/nclimgrid-daily), 98 counties had their highest county-average daily maximum temperature in the 76-year period of record (1951–2026), representing 6.7% of the CONUS area and an estimated population of 6.1 million people (based on 2020 U.S. Census data).

The CONUS [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/1/7/1895-2026) was 64.2°F, 3.7°F above average, [ranking as the warmest month](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmin/202607#1) on record for average low temperatures, surpassing July 2022 by 0.7°F. Elevated overnight temperatures were exceptionally widespread, with above-average minimums spanning nearly the entire CONUS and pockets of record warmth observed across parts of the West, Rockies, Upper Midwest, Deep South and Southeast.

Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jul/1-month), the CONUS temperature-related energy demand during July was 201% of average and the eighth-highest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### July Precipitation

[![Image 16: July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202607.png) July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202607.png "July 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The [total precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) averaged across the CONUS in July was 2.55 inches, 0.23 inch below the 20th-century average, ranking in the [driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202607#1) of the 132-year record and the driest July since 2012.

Precipitation across the CONUS during July reflected a mix of wet and dry conditions. Below-average precipitation occurred across portions of the northern tier, including parts of the northern Rockies, northern Plains, Upper Midwest and Northeast, as well as parts of the southern Plains, Mississippi Valley, central Gulf and Southeast. In contrast, pockets of above-average precipitation were observed across parts of the West and Southwest, central Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as portions of Texas, the Tennessee and lower Ohio valleys, Mid-Atlantic and lower Northeast.

The regional precipitation contrasts were particularly evident across the Northeast. Statewide, [Maine](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/17/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) had its fourth-driest July on record (46% below average), while [Connecticut](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/6/pcp/1/7/1895-2026), [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) and [Massachusetts](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/19/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) recorded their sixth-, seventh- and 12th-wettest July on record, respectively, with precipitation 72% to 105% above average.

[Precipitation across Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/1/7/1925-2026) in July averaged 4.30 inches, 1.02 inches above the 1925–2000 average, [ranking in the wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/50/pcp/202607#1) of the 102-year record. Southern and southwestern portions of the state, including the Alaska Peninsula, received above-average to much-above-average precipitation, with Anchorage tying its highest July precipitation total on record. In contrast, portions of the Alaska Panhandle received below-average precipitation.

[Precipitation across Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/1/7/1895-2026) in July averaged 5.20 inches, 0.56 inch above the 1991–2020 average, [ranking in the wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/51/pcp/202607#1) of the 36-year record. Despite the above-average statewide precipitation, localized dry conditions occurred across parts of the islands, with Honolulu receiving just 0.02 inch of rainfall, tying its driest July on record.

#### Drought

According to the August 4 [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx), about 48.5% of the CONUS was in drought, an increase of about 0.7 percentage points since the end of June. Drought persisted over much of the interior West, Southwest and Rockies, and expanded or intensified across parts of the Northwest, southern and northern Plains, Upper Midwest and far Northeast. In contrast, drought contracted or decreased in intensity across portions of the Lower Mississippi Valley, Tennessee Valley and much of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic region. In Puerto Rico, more than two-thirds of the island was in drought, with more than one-third classified as severe drought or worse.

See the accompanying national [Drought Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/drought/202607) for further details.

#### Other Notable Events

Several notable events in July included:

*   **Northern Rockies and West:** A heat wave on July 12 brought all-time record high temperatures to multiple airport stations across Idaho, Utah, Wyoming and Montana, including Idaho Falls, ID (103°F), Salt Lake City, UT (109°F), Sheridan, WY (109°F), Billings, MT (111°F) and Miles City, MT (115°F).
*   **Wyoming:** Boysen Dam recorded a monthly average temperature of 81.3°F in July, setting an all-time record for the highest monthly average temperature observed at any weather station in Wyoming history. _See the High Plains RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Oregon:** Wildfires across eastern Oregon burned more than 140,000 acres in July, triggering local evacuations and regional air quality hazards.
*   **Southwest:** Elevated overnight temperatures in late July set an all-time record warm low temperature of 99°F in Laughlin, Nevada, and tied record warm low temperatures in Phoenix, Arizona (97°F), and Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada (96°F).
*   **Nebraska and South Dakota:** A late-July heat wave featuring heat index values above 120°F and light winds led to an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 cattle fatalities across Nebraska and South Dakota. _See the High Plains RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Iowa:** Back-to-back heavy rainfall events during July 2–4 dropped 5 to 10 inches of rain across central Iowa, causing major flash flooding in Polk, Story and Jasper counties and driving Fourmile Creek near Des Moines to its second-highest crest on record. _See the [NWS Des Moines, IA summary](https://www.weather.gov/dmx/July\_2\_4\_2026\_Flash\_Flooding) and Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Michigan:** A high-instability squall line on July 3 swept across Lower Michigan with wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph, causing tree damage and knocking out electrical power to nearly 400,000 utility customers in the Detroit metro area. _See the [NWS Detroit, MI summary](https://www.weather.gov/dtx/severeweather070326) for additional details._
*   **Missouri:** On July 4, a line of severe thunderstorms produced estimated straight-line wind gusts up to 105 mph east of Jefferson City to Osage City along the Missouri River corridor, causing structural and tree damage across Cole, Callaway and Osage counties. _See the [NWS St. Louis, MO summary](https://www.weather.gov/lsx/7\_4\_26) for additional details._
*   **Illinois, Kentucky and Missouri:** Training thunderstorms during July 9–11 produced a broad swath of 6 to 11 inches of rainfall across southern Illinois, western Kentucky and southeastern Missouri, triggering flash flooding and washed-out roadways. _See the [NWS Paducah, KY summary](https://www.weather.gov/pah/July9-11\_2026\_Flooding\_Severe) and Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Upper Midwest:** Canadian wildfire smoke transported into the central U.S. during mid-July produced Minnesota's worst air quality outbreak in at least 50 years. _See the Midwest RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Wisconsin and Illinois:** An outbreak of severe weather on July 27 produced an EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 140 mph that tracked through Fox Crossing and Menasha in the Appleton, Wisconsin area, injuring at least 60 people before moving over Lake Winnebago as a waterspout. The storm system also produced seven tornadoes and 80 to 100 mph straight-line wind gusts across the Chicago metro area. _See the [NWS Green Bay, WI summary](https://www.weather.gov/grb/07272026\_SevereStorms), [NWS Chicago, IL summary](https://www.weather.gov/lot/2026\_07\_27\_severe\_flood) and the accompanying [Tornadoes Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202607) for additional details._
*   **Texas Hill Country:** Persistent, heavy rainfall during July 13–17 dropped up to 28.23 inches of rain near Knippa, Texas, triggering major flash flooding across multiple river basins. The [Nueces River below Uvalde](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/flood_UVLT2_20260714-20260719.png) reached a record major flood crest of 28.01 feet on July 16, breaking its 1996 record of 24.88 feet. _See the preliminary [WPC Storm Summary](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/storm\_summaries/storm11/stormsum\_6.html) and the Southern RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Galveston, Texas:** On July 31, Galveston Scholes Field reached 100°F, marking its first triple-digit temperature ever recorded during the month of July in over a century of observations. _See the Southern RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Carolinas, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast:** Numerous locations observed their warmest July 4 on record during an early-July heat wave stretching from Highlands, NC, to Cape Cod, MA. Daily maximum temperature records included Raleigh, NC (103°F), Washington, D.C. (103°F), Danville, VA (103°F) and Richmond, VA (100°F). Atlantic City, NJ, reached 106°F during the early-July heat wave, tying its all-time highest temperature on record. _See the Northeast RCC Report and Southeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **West Virginia:** A severe storm outbreak on July 21 produced nine tornadoes across West Virginia—one of the state's most active tornado days since 1950—and 4 to 8 inches of rainfall, triggering a Flash Flood Emergency in Upshur County where Sand Run at Buckhannon reached its highest river crest on record. _See the Northeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **North Carolina:** Raleigh-Durham International Airport recorded 12.16 inches of rain in July (its second-wettest July on record), receiving more precipitation in a single month than during the entire January–June period combined (11.88 inches) and alleviating severe drought along the I-85/40 corridor. _See the Southeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Northeast and Mid-Atlantic:** Slow-moving thunderstorms on July 28–29 produced widespread flash flooding from eastern Pennsylvania to southern New England. Storm total rainfall reached nearly 12 inches in eastern New York, with 1,000-year rainfall recurrence intervals observed in Schodack (11.80 in) and Kinderhook (11.48 in). Albany, NY (5.45 in) and Worcester, MA (4.56 in) each set all-time daily rainfall records for the month of July on July 29. _See the [NWS Binghamton, NY summary](https://www.weather.gov/bgm/pastRainfallJuly29\_August032026) and Northeast RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Alaska:** Cool and wet conditions prevailed across much of southern Alaska, with Talkeetna recording its wettest July since 1922 (10.59 in) and Anchorage tying 2001 for its wettest July on record (4.49 in). Cold Bay recorded an 85-year monthly record low temperature of 32°F on July 6. Additionally, end-of-July sea ice extent in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas was the highest since 2000 and 2003, respectively. _See the Western RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Hawaiʻi:** Unseasonably dry conditions prevailed across parts of the islands during July, with Honolulu receiving just 0.02 inch of rainfall, tying its driest July on record. _See the Western RCC Report for additional details._
*   **Puerto Rico:** San Juan recorded its driest July in 128 years of observations with just 0.54 inch of rain, breaking the previous record of 1.10 inches set in 1929. According to the August 4 U.S. Drought Monitor, more than two-thirds of Puerto Rico was in drought, with more than one-third of the island classified as severe drought or worse. _See the Southeast RCC Report for additional details._

For additional details of notable July events please refer to the Regional Climate Center summaries below.

#### January–July Temperature

[![Image 22: January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202607.png) January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202607.png "January–July 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/ytd/7/1895-2026) for the CONUS during January–July was 55.5°F, 4.2°F above the 20th-century average. The period [ranked second warmest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202607#7) in the 132-year record, 0.17°F cooler than January–July 2012. Most of the CONUS saw above- to much-above-average temperatures, with 30 states ranking among their 10 warmest January–July periods on record. Eight states recorded their warmest January–July period on record.

Based on the [NOAA climate regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/mapping/-1/tavg/202607/ytd/rank), the West and Southwest each experienced their warmest January–July period on record, while the South ranked second warmest, the Northern Rockies and Plains third warmest and the Northwest region fourth warmest. The [Southwest region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/time-series/107/tavg/7/7/1895-2026) was especially anomalous, averaging 6.0°F above its 20th-century January–July baseline and eclipsing the previous record, tied in 2000 and 2018, by 2.1°F.

At the county level, [more than 450 counties](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/county/mapping/110/tavg/202607/ytd/rank)—covering over one-quarter of the CONUS and affecting an estimated 72 million people—recorded their warmest January–July on record, reflecting the broad geographic footprint of the period's record warmth.

The CONUS average [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/ytd/7/1895-2026) was 67.9°F, 4.7°F above average, and the average [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/ytd/7/1895-2026) was 43.0°F, 3.8°F above average, with both measures ranking second warmest on record. Averaged over the entire [Rockies and Westward region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/reference-maps/rockies-and-westward), the January–July period set new records, with an average maximum temperature 0.7°F above the 1934 Dust Bowl-era record and an average minimum temperature 0.6°F above the 2015 record.

Based on [REDTI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jul/year-to-date), the temperature-related energy demand for CONUS from January through July was 37% of average and the 10th-lowest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### January–July Precipitation

The average [precipitation total](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) across the CONUS during January–July was 16.28 inches, 1.80 inches below the 20th-century average, [ranking in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202607#7) of the 132-year record and the driest January–July since 2012.

Much of the western half of the CONUS received below- to much-below-average precipitation during January–July, along with parts of the Lower Mississippi and Tennessee valleys, Southeast, Mid-Atlantic and coastal areas of the Northeast. In contrast, portions of the Midwest and Great Lakes received above-average precipitation. These regional differences were reflected in statewide rankings; for example, [South Carolina](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/38/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) (67.1% of average) ranked third driest while [Michigan](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/20/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) (131.9% of average) ranked third wettest.

Above-average precipitation was observed across much of the Alaska mainland, while portions of the Aleutians and parts of the Panhandle received below-average precipitation.

In Hawaiʻi, [year-to-date precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/ytd/7/1895-2026) totaled 59.82 inches, 25.43 inches above the 1991–2020 average (173.9% of average), ranking as the [wettest January–July](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/haywood/51/pcp/12) in the 36-year record.

#### Extremes

The year-to-date [USCEI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/) was 137% above the long-term average, ranking as the second-highest January–July value in the 117-year record. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/1) spanned 78% of the CONUS, the second-largest extent on record, while warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/2) covered 73% of the CONUS, the third-largest extent on record. [Dry extremes](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/3), as measured by low Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) values, covered 45% of the CONUS, ranking as the second-largest January–July extent on record, behind 1934 during the Dust Bowl era.

[Regionally](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/cei-hi), the Southwest and South set their highest January–July CEI values on record, while the West ranked second highest and the Ohio Valley fourth highest for the period. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/1-hi) broke several January–July records, covering the entire West and Southwest regions (100%), along with 92% of the South (record high) and 97% of the Northwest (fourth highest). Warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/2-hi) were also widespread, covering more than 98% of the West, Southwest and South, each a record high for the period, and 93% of the Northwest (third highest). The spatial extent of [very low PDSI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/3-lo) values set January–July records in the Southwest (96%) and Southeast (67%), and was much above average across the West, Northwest, South, Ohio Valley and Northeast (second highest). In contrast, extreme 1-day precipitation totals set a January–July record in the [Ohio Valley](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/ce/ytd/4), covering 39% of the region.

#### Monthly Outlook

Above-average August [temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdotempoutlook-202607.gif) are favored across the central and southern tiers of the CONUS, with portions of coastal California and the southern Plains having a greater than 50% likelihood of above-average temperatures. [Precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdoprcpoutlook-202607.gif) has equal chances of being above or below average across much of the CONUS, except in parts of the interior West and Southwest where above-average rainfall is favored and in portions of the southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley where below-average precipitation is favored. Visit the Climate Prediction Center's [Official 30-Day Forecasts](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/30day/) for more details.

[Drought](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/usdodroughtoutlook-202607.png) is expected to persist and expand across parts of the Northwest and east of the Rockies, including portions of the Plains and Upper Midwest, as well as in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Drought conditions are expected to improve across parts of the interior West and Southwest, and along much of the eastern seaboard. Visit the [U.S. Monthly Drought Outlook](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/expert_assessment/mdo_summary.php) website for more details.

Significant wildland [fire potential for August](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jul/nifcfireoutlook-202607.png) is above normal across the Northwest, Great Basin and central Rockies, parts of the northern and southern Plains, the Lower Mississippi Valley, southern Florida and Puerto Rico. For additional information on wildland fire potential, visit the [National Interagency Fire Center](https://www.nifc.gov/) website.

### Regional Highlights

These regional summaries were provided by the six [Regional Climate Centers](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/regional/regional-climate-centers) and reflect conditions in their respective regions. These six regions differ spatially from the [nine climatic regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/reference-maps/us-climate-regions) of the National Centers for Environmental Information.

#### Northeast _(Information provided by the [Northeast Regional Climate Center](http://www.nrcc.cornell.edu/))_

July in the Northeast featured a record-setting heat wave, locally extreme rainfall, and several significant severe weather events.

**Read the full Northeast RCC report...**
##### **Temperature**

The average temperature for July in the Northeast was 71.1°F, 0.9°F hotter than normal. July average temperatures for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 0.4°F below normal in Connecticut to 1.8°F above normal in West Virginia, with nine of the states being warmer than normal. This July ranked as the 14th hottest July since recordkeeping began in 1895 for Delaware and as the 17th hottest on record for Maryland and West Virginia. A heat wave in early July set or tied multiple records. Atlantic City, New Jersey, tied its all-time hottest temperature of 106°F, while Wilmington, Delaware, tied its hottest July temperature of 103°F. Low temperatures of 84°F at Washington, D.C.; 80°F at Providence, Rhode Island; and 71°F at Caribou, Maine, tied as each site's all-time hottest low temperatures on record. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and Dulles Airport, Virginia, tied their hottest low temperatures for July at 81°F and 78°F, respectively. Several other notable records were set/tied including longest streak of days with a high of 100°F or higher. See the Notable Weather Events section below for more information. On July 16, Dulles Airport, Virginia, had a low of 81°F: its first time on record with a low of at least 80°F, the hottest low temperature for July beating the record set earlier in the month, and its hottest low temperature for any month on record.

##### **Precipitation**

During July, the Northeast received 4.53 inches of precipitation, which was 104% of normal. Precipitation during July for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 51% of normal in Maine to 198% of normal in Rhode Island, with eight states being wetter than normal. This July was the fourth-driest July for Maine but ranked among the 20 wettest for five other states: Connecticut, sixth wettest; Rhode Island, seventh wettest; Massachusetts, 12th wettest; Delaware, 15th wettest; and New Jersey, 18th wettest. On July 29, Albany, New York, had 5.45 inches of rain and Worcester, Massachusetts, saw 4.56 inches of rain, qualifying as each site's wettest July day on record.

##### **Drought**

The U.S. Drought Monitor from July 7 showed 25% of the Northeast in drought and 12% of the region as abnormally dry. Extreme drought was present in portions of Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey, while severe and/or moderate drought were found in locations closer to the coast along a path from Maryland to Maine, as well as some southern locations like southern and eastern West Virginia. During July, drought contracted in areas that saw ample rainfall and recovering streamflow, groundwater levels and soil moisture. For example, extreme drought was erased from much of Maryland and New Jersey, while severe drought in West Virginia, New York, and Rhode Island was reduced to small patches. The notable exception was Maine, where moderate drought spread due to reduced rainfall and declining streamflow, groundwater levels, and soil moisture. The U.S. Drought Monitor from July 28 showed 21% of the Northeast in drought and 18% of the region as abnormally dry. Drought conditions continued to have impacts in the region. At times during July, USGS 7-day streamflow was record low in places like the Delmarva Peninsula, southeastern Pennsylvania, coastal New Jersey, central New York, and central Maine. Groundwater levels were record low at times during the month in several areas including parts of Maryland, southeastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, eastern New York, and southeastern Massachusetts. Water conservation continued to be encouraged in some areas, with a few water suppliers in parts of southern New Hampshire, southern New England, southeastern New York, northeastern New Jersey, and south-central Pennsylvania having mandatory water restrictions or watering bans. In early July, a report from southwestern West Virginia noted that people continued to fill water tanks at the municipal water source. Baltimore, Maryland, officials tested their backup water system for the first time in 20 years. Drought and hot temperatures contributed to a fishkill in the Potomac River in Maryland. Condition monitoring reports from West Virginia during the month noted that hot, dry weather slowed crop and pasture growth and left fields dry, second cutting of hay yields were reduced (in some locations by over 50%) compared to an average year, and that a grower opted to have cattle graze a hay field instead of cutting it due to drought. Additionally, some corn crops in Delaware were a loss.

##### **Notable Weather**

From July 1–5, the Northeast experienced a record-setting heat wave. For the first time on record, Atlantic City, New Jersey, had three straight days with a high of at least 103°F, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, had three consecutive days with a high of at least 101°F. Atlantic City and Philadelphia had their greatest number of days with a high of at least 103°F and at least 101°F, respectively, for any month on record. It became the only July on record to have three consecutive days with a high of at least 102°F in Wilmington, Delaware. Several sites including Kennedy Airport, New York; Harrisburg, Pennsylvania; and Boston, Massachusetts, had their longest streak of days with a high of at least 100°F. Both Atlantic City and Kennedy Airport set/tied their record for greatest number of days with a high of at least 100°F for any month on record with 4 days and 3 days, respectively. Similarly, Wilmington and LaGuardia Airport, New York, set/tied their record for greatest number of days with a high of at least 100°F for July, with 3 days and 2 days, respectively. For the first time in July, Providence, Rhode Island, had a low of at least 80°F, which also tied as its greatest number of such days for any month on record. Portland, Maine, had back-to-back days with a low of at least 72°F, tying its longest such streak. Preliminary data indicated that PJM Interconnection, a power grid operator that services over 65 million customers and covers much of the Mid-Atlantic, set a record for its highest peak load on July 2. The heat caused several Fourth of July events to be cancelled and was linked to at least 39 deaths and hundreds of people seeking heat-related medical care.

There were several other significant events in July. A preliminary total of 37 tornadoes were reported in the Northeast. This included 14 tornadoes in Pennsylvania, well above the state's July average of three tornadoes (based on data from 2001–2025). West Virginia had nine tornadoes compared to its July average of zero, while Maryland had six tornadoes compared to its July average of one. New York had five tornadoes, while New Jersey had four, compared to their July averages of three tornadoes and one tornado, respectively. Preliminary data indicated a few counties including Morris County in New Jersey, Broome County in New York, Pendleton and Pleasants Counties in West Virginia, and Anne Arundel and Talbot Counties in Maryland set or tied their record for greatest number of tornadoes for any month and/or year, with records back to 1950. During the month, there were hundreds of instances of wind damage across the region, along with some large hail.

### Introduction

Temperature anomalies and percentiles are shown on the gridded maps below. The anomaly map on the left and the percentiles map on the right are a product of a merged land surface temperature ([Global Historical Climatology Network, GHCN](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/data-access/land-based-station-data/land-based-datasets/global-historical-climatology-network-monthly-version-4)) and sea surface temperature ([ERSST version 5](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/data-access/marineocean-data/extended-reconstructed-sea-surface-temperature-ersst-v5)) anomaly analysis. The anomalies maps tell us whether the temperature observed for a specific place and time period was warmer or cooler than a reference value and by how much. While the percentile map provides additional information by placing the temperature anomaly observed into historical perspective, showing how the most current month, season or year compares with the past. Temperature anomalies for land and ocean are analyzed separately and then merged to form the global analysis. For more information, please visit NCEI's [Global Surface Temperature Anomalies page](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-references/faq/anomalies.php).

### Temperature

In the atmosphere, 500-millibar height pressure anomalies correlate well with temperatures at the Earth's surface. The average position of the upper-level ridges of high pressure and troughs of low pressure—depicted by positive and negative 500-millibar height anomalies on the [July 2020](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/service/global/hgtanomaly-global/202007.png "July 2020 500 millibar height anomalies") map—is generally reflected by areas of positive and negative temperature anomalies at the surface, respectively.

#### Monthly Temperature: July 2020

The [July 2020 global land and ocean surface temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/globe/land_ocean/1/7/1880-2020) of 0.92°C (1.66°F) above the 20th century average tied with 2016 as the second highest July global temperature since records began in 1880. This value was only 0.01°C (0.02°F) shy of tying the record warm July of 2019. July 2020 was the 44th consecutive July and the 427th consecutive month with temperatures, at least nominally, above the 20th century average. Nine of the 10 warmest Julys on record have occurred since 2010. The six warmest Julys on record have occurred since 2015.

[![Image 4: /monitoring-content/sotc/global/2020/jul/global-land-ocean-anomalies-202007.png](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/2020/jul/global-land-ocean-anomalies-202007.png)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/2020/jul/global-land-ocean-anomalies-202007.png)

The month was characterized by warmer-than-average temperatures across much of the global land and ocean surface. The most notable warm temperature departures of +2.0°C (+3.6°F) were present across the North Pacific Ocean, the southwestern and northeastern contiguous U.S., eastern Canada, and across parts of western Asia and eastern Antarctica. Record-warm July temperatures were widespread across the North Indian Ocean, southeastern Asia, and the western Pacific Ocean. Other areas with record-warm July temperatures were present across parts of the Caribbean Sea, northern South America, North America, and the North Pacific Ocean. Overall, [July 2020 had 8.67% of the world's land and ocean surfaces with a record July temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/global/202007/supplemental/page-4). This was the second highest percentage for July record warm temperatures across the globe since records began in 1951, behind July 2015 (10.23%).

According to the July 2020 percentiles map, cooler-than-average July temperatures were limited to small parts of northern North America, the northern Atlantic Ocean, Scandinavia, eastern China, southern South America, and the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. No land or ocean areas had a record-cold July temperature.

[![Image 5: July 2020 Blended Land and Sea Surface Temperature Anomalies in degrees Celsius](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/map-blended-mntp/map-blended-mntp-202007.png) July 2020 Blended Land and Sea Surface Temperature Anomalies in degrees Celsius](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/map-blended-mntp/map-blended-mntp-202007.png)

[![Image 6: July 2020 Blended Land and Sea Surface Temperature Percentiles](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/map-percentile-mntp/map-percentile-mntp-202007.png) July 2020 Blended Land and Sea Surface Temperature Percentiles](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/global/map-percentile-mntp/map-percentile-mntp-202007.png)

The [global land-only surface temperature for July 2020](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/globe/land/1/7/1880-2020) was the second highest on record at 1.23°C (2.21°F) above average and only 0.01°C (0.02°F) less than the record-warm July set in 2017. The [global ocean-only surface temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/globe/ocean/1/7/1880-2020) was the third highest on record at 0.80°C (1.44°F) above average. Only July 2016 and 2019 had a higher global ocean surface temperature.

The [Northern Hemisphere land and ocean surface temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/nhem/land_ocean/1/7/1880-2020) was the highest in the 141-year record at 1.18°C (2.12°F) above average. This was 0.08°C (0.14°F) higher than the now second warmest July of 2019.

Regionally, the [Caribbean region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/caribbeanIslands/land_ocean/1/7/1910-2020) had its warmest July on record, with a temperature departure of 1.24°C (2.23°F) above average. This was 0.09°C (0.16°F) above the previous record set in 2016. The Caribbean region's five warmest Julys have occurred since 1998.

[North America](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/northAmerica/land/1/7/1910-2020) had its second warmest July on record at 1.31°C (2.36°F) above average. Only July of 2012 was warmer at 1.74°C (3.13°F). Asia had its third warmest July, while Africa and South America had their seventh and ninth warmest July in the 111-year continental record, respectively.

#### Year-to-date Temperature: January–July 2020

The [January–July global land and ocean surface temperature departure](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cag/global/time-series/globe/land_ocean/ytd/7/1880-2020) was 1.05°C (1.89°F) above average and the second warmest such period in the 141-year record. Only the year-to-date period of 2016 is warmer by 0.04°C (0.07°F). According to a statistical analysis done by NCEI scientist, the year 2020 is very likely to rank among the five warmest years on record.

This value surpassed the previous record set in 2014 by +0.12°C (+0.22°F). Europe's five warmest January–Julys on record have occurred since 2014.

For Asia, the year-to-date temperature departure of +2.57°C (+4.63°F) surpassed the now second warmest January–July set in 2016 by +0.48°C (0.86°F). Only January–July of 2016 and 2020 have a temperature departure surpassing 2.0°C (3.6°F).

The Gulf of Mexico had a temperature that was 0.97°C (1.75°F) above average and the highest since regional records began in 1910. This value surpassed the previous record set in 1943 and again in 2017 by +0.10°C (+0.18°F).
