#### May Temperature

[![Image 6: May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202505.png) May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202505.png "May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/1/5/1895-2025) for the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) in May 2025 was 61.7°F, 1.5°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202505#1) of the 131-year period of record. Much of the West, Southwest and Northwest, as well as the northern Rockies and Plains, recorded above-average temperatures. Warmer-than-normal conditions also extended along the southern Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida and up the entire Atlantic seaboard. [Florida](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/8/tavg/1/5/1895-2025) experienced its second-warmest May on record at 4.0°F above average, while [California](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/4/tavg/1/5/1895-2025) was 3.9°F above average, tying for its ninth-warmest May. In contrast, temperatures across the central U.S. were generally near- to below-average.

The CONUS average [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/1/5/1895-2025) in May was 74.1°F, 1.1°F above average, while the average [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/1/5/1895-2025) was 49.4°F, 1.9°F above average; both ranked in the warmest third of the historical record. The spatial pattern of temperature anomalies showed a distinct contrast: [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-tmax-202505.png) were above average across the western third of the country, as well as parts of the northern Plains, southern Texas and Florida, while a broad swath from the central U.S. to the Appalachians and into the Northeast experienced cooler-than-average daytime highs. A similar pattern was observed in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-tmin-202505.png). However, the cooler anomalies were mostly confined to parts of the southern Rockies, central Plains and middle Mississippi Valley, while the entire Atlantic coastal region recorded warmer-than-average overnight lows.

The average [temperature for Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/tavg/1/5/1925-2025) in May was 39.0°F, 1.2°F above the long-term average, ranking in the middle third of the 101-year record. [Average temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-ak-tavg-202505.png) varied across the state, with parts of the northern and eastern regions experiencing below-average conditions—particularly in daytime [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-ak-tmax-202505.png). Notably, temperatures in Utqiaġvik remained below freezing for the entire month—a first since May 2007. In contrast, much of the southern interior was warmer than normal, especially with respect to overnight [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-ak-tmin-202505.png).

The [average temperature for Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/tavg/1/5/1895-2025) in May was 66.5°F, 0.3°F above the 1991–2020 average. [Minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-hi-tmin-202505.png) were mostly above average—especially across the western islands—while average daytime [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-hi-tmax-202505.png) were slightly below average. Nonetheless, several co-op observing sites reported their highest May temperatures on record, including Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site, which recorded an average of 80.8°F for the month, the highest since records began in 1977.

Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/may/1-month), the contiguous U.S. temperature-related energy demand during May was 90 percent of average, ranking near the middle of the 131-year period of record.

#### May Precipitation

[![Image 7: May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202505.png) May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202505.png "May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The [total precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/1/5/1895-2025) averaged across the CONUS in May was 3.63 inches, 0.72 inch above the 20th-century average, ranking in the [wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202505#1) of the 131-year record for the month.

There was a distinct contrast in [precipitation anomalies](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-prcp/grid-ranks-prcp-202505.png) across the U.S. during May, with some regions much wetter and others drier than average. Much of the South and East Coast experienced notably wet conditions, with the [Southeast](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/time-series/104/pcp/1/5/1895-2025) region recording its second-wettest May and the [Northeast](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/time-series/101/pcp/1/5/1895-2025) its third-wettest. [Alabama](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/1/pcp/1/5/1895-2025) had its wettest May on record—its first with more than 10 inches of rainfall—while Maryland, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Vermont each recorded their second-wettest. In total, 12 states in the Lower 48 experienced one of their five wettest Mays, and 49 counties recorded the wettest May on record—home to more than 4 million people, based on 2020 Census data. Precipitation was also above average in parts of the Southwest and northern Plains, while drier-than-average conditions prevailed along portions of the Pacific Coast, the Northwest and the upper Mississippi Valley.

[Precipitation varied across Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/divisionalpcpnrank/divisionakpcpnrank-202505-202505.png), but overall the state experienced its [second-wettest May on record](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/1/5/1925-2025)—just shy of the record in 1944—largely due to exceptionally heavy rainfall in the Southeast region, where many long-term stations set new precipitation records for the month of May.

In Hawaiʻi, [May precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/1/5/1895-2025) averaged 3.17 inches, 0.91 inch below average, ranking in the middle third of the 35-year record. [Rainfall varied across the islands](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-prcp/prcp-diff-hi-202505.png), with wetter-than-average conditions in the west and drier-than-average conditions in the east.

#### Drought

According to the June 3 [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx), about 29.6% of the contiguous U.S. was in drought, a decrease of approximately 7.4% since the end of April. Drought conditions contracted or decreased in intensity along much of the East Coast, from Florida to the Northeast. Improvements were also observed in parts of the Southwest and across sections of the southern, central and northern Plains. In contrast, drought developed or intensified across parts of the Northwest, central Rockies, middle Mississippi Valley and Great Lakes regions. In Hawaiʻi, drought conditions improved over the western islands but intensified over the Big Island.

#### Other Notable Events

*   Two significant severe weather outbreaks on May 15–16 and May 18–20 brought over 200 tornado reports, along with very large hail and damaging winds. Please refer to the full [tornado report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/monthly-report/tornadoes/202505) for further details on tornadoes in May. 
*   On May 16, strong winds gusted through northern Illinois and Indiana, driving the largest [dust storm](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/noaa-satellites-watch-dust-storm-sweep-across-the-midwest) to impact the Chicago area since the 1930s Dust Bowl era. 
*   Just before Memorial Day weekend, a rare May nor'easter brought heavy rain to the Northeast, snow to New Hampshire's higher elevations, and set record-cold daytime high temperatures at several sites. 
*   In late May, a heatwave impacted parts of California and Nevada, setting several daily temperature records—including 99°F on May 31 at Reno-Tahoe Airport, the hottest May temperature since records began in 1888. 
*   Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania, recorded its wettest May on record with 13.26 inches of rain, measured on 22 days—including five days with one inch or more. 

For additional details of notable May events please refer to the regional summaries below.

#### March–May Temperature

[![Image 10: March–May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202503-202505.png) March–May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202503-202505.png "March–May 2025 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

During meteorological spring (March–May) 2025, the CONUS [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/3/5/1895-2025) was 54.1°F, 3.2°F above average, making it the [second-warmest spring](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202505#3) in the 131-year record. North Carolina recorded its second-warmest spring (3.7°F above average), while Georgia, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi and Virginia each matched or exceeded their third-warmest spring on record. In total, 66 counties matched or surpassed the warmest spring on record—home to more than 16 million people based on 2020 Census data.

The CONUS average [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/3/5/1895-2025) for March–May was 66.7°F, 3.6°F above average, the [fourth warmest on record](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmax/202505#3) for this period, while the average spring [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/3/5/1895-2025) was 41.5°F, 2.8°F above average—[ranking fifth warmest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmin/202505#3) for the season.

[Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/tavg/3/5/1925-2025)'s average temperature for the March–May season was 27.7°F, which is 3.7°F above average and ranks in the warmest third of the historical record. Spring [average temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-ak-tavg-202503-202505.png) were above the long-term average across much of the state.

In [Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/tavg/3/5/1895-2025), the average temperature for March–May was 65.7°F, 0.9°F above average, tying for the fifth-warmest spring in the 35-year period of record. Warmer-than-average [spring temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-hi-tmin-202503-202505.png) were observed across much of the island chain, with several stations reporting their warmest spring on record—including Honolulu International and Molokaʻi airports.

Based on [REDTI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/may/3-month), the temperature-related energy demand for CONUS during spring was 32 percent of average and the sixth-lowest value in the 131-year period of record.

#### March–May Precipitation

[![Image 11: March–May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202503-202505.png) March–May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202503-202505.png "March–May 2025 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

During spring, the CONUS received an average of 8.90 inches of [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/3/5/1895-2025), 0.97 inch above the long-term average, ranking in the wettest third of the 131-year record. Much-above-average precipitation fell across parts of the southern Plains, South, Ohio Valley, and Northeast, as well as portions of the northern Plains and upper Great Lakes. In contrast, below-average precipitation was observed in parts of the Mountain West, central Plains, and across the Florida Peninsula.

[Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/3/5/1925-2025) tied its second-wettest March–May period on record—the wettest spring since 1963—despite some parts of the West Coast and western Aleutians being drier than average.

In [Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/3/5/1895-2025), March–May precipitation totaled 11.51 inches, which is 4.43 inches below the 1991-2020 average and ranks in the driest third of the 35-year record.

#### Extremes

The [U.S. Climate Extremes Index (USCEI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/) tracks extremes (occurring in the upper or lower 10 percent of the historical record) in temperature, precipitation and drought across the contiguous United States. The USCEI was 50 percent above average across the CONUS for the spring (March–May) season, ranking in the upper third of the record. Warm extremes in maximum and minimum temperatures affected more than four times the expected area during spring, while no areas experienced cool seasonal extremes. The wet-dry contrast across the CONUS during spring was pronounced, with [record extremes in 1-day rainfall](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/03-05/4) and larger-than-expected areas with unusually dry conditions, as indicated by a low Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI).

Most [regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2025/03-05/cei-hi) across the country saw elevated CEI composite values for March–May. Warm spring temperature extremes were observed across all regions, except in the West and Upper Midwest, where the areas experiencing warm maximum and minimum temperatures, respectively, were smaller than expected. Several regions experienced widespread spring dryness, with large areas of extremely low PDSI values—most notably in the [Southwest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/sw/03-05/3) and [West](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/we/03-05/3). In contrast, the [Northeast](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/ne/03-05/5) had nearly six times the expected area receiving frequent precipitation—its third highest in the 116-year record, based on the number of days with precipitation. Additionally, all regions except the Southwest experienced elevated extremes in 1-day precipitation extremes, with a record two-thirds of the [Northwest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/nw/03-05/4) observing 1-day precipitation extremes.

### Regional Highlights

These regional summaries were provided by the six [Regional Climate Centers](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/regional/regional-climate-centers) and reflect conditions in their respective regions. These six regions differ spatially from the [nine climatic regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/reference-maps/us-climate-regions) of the National Centers for Environmental Information.

#### Northeast _(Information provided by the [Northeast Regional Climate Center](http://www.nrcc.cornell.edu/))_

A soggy May with variable temperatures rounded out a mild, wet spring, resulting in reduced drought coverage across the Northeast.

##### Temperature

The Northeast's average temperature for May of 56.9°F was exactly normal. State average temperatures for May ranged from 0.7°F below normal in West Virginia to 1.5°F above normal in Delaware, which had its 18th warmest May. Overall, nine of the 12 Northeast states averaged out to be warmer than normal. The Northeast had its 10th warmest spring since recordkeeping began in 1895, with an average temperature of 48.0°F, 2.2°F above normal. This spring ranked among the 20 warmest on record for all 12 Northeast states: Maryland, third warmest; Delaware and Rhode Island, fourth warmest; New Jersey, sixth warmest; Connecticut and Massachusetts, seventh warmest; Pennsylvania and West Virginia, 11th warmest; New Hampshire and Vermont, 12th warmest; New York, 13th warmest; and Maine, 20th warmest. Spring average temperatures for the states ranged from 1.8°F above normal in Maine to 3.1°F above normal in Maryland.

##### Precipitation

May 2025 ranked as the third-wettest May since 1895 for the Northeast, with 6.31 inches of precipitation, 159 percent of normal. May precipitation for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 122 percent of normal in Maine to 236 percent of normal in Rhode Island. This May ranked among the 11 wettest on record for all but Maine: Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island, second wettest; Massachusetts; third wettest; New Hampshire, fourth wettest; New Jersey, sixth wettest; Connecticut, Delaware, and Vermont, seventh wettest; West Virginia, eighth wettest; and New York, 11th wettest. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, had its wettest May since 1889 with 10.02 inches of precipitation, beating its old record of 9.71 inches from 1989. The Northeast had its 17th-wettest spring on record, seeing 13.16 inches of precipitation, 117 percent of normal. Spring precipitation for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 99 percent of normal in West Virginia, the lone drier-than-normal state, to 135 percent of normal in Delaware. This spring ranked among the 20 wettest springs on record for eight states: Massachusetts, eighth wettest; Delaware and Vermont, ninth wettest; New Hampshire, 11th wettest; Rhode Island, 14th wettest; Maine, 15th wettest; Maryland, 17th wettest; and Pennsylvania, 19th wettest.

##### Drought

The U.S. Drought Monitor from May 6 showed 13 percent of the Northeast in drought and 19 percent of the region as abnormally dry. Severe and moderate drought were present in an area from eastern West Virginia to southeastern New York, with moderate drought also in parts of southern New Jersey and coastal New England. Abnormal dryness existed in all 12 Northeast states. Abundant precipitation in May allowed drought and abnormal dryness to contract across the region. Severe drought eased in all but central Maryland, while moderate drought was erased from or contracted in the eight states where it was present. Abnormal dryness also eased or contracted in all states. At month's end, drought was generally focused in an area extending from eastern West Virginia through Maryland into southeastern Pennsylvania. During May, New Hampshire became free of both drought and abnormal dryness for the first time since June 2024. Meanwhile, for the first time since fall 2024, Vermont and Rhode Island became free of drought and abnormal dryness, while Maine, New York, and New Jerey became drought free. The U.S. Drought Monitor from May 27 showed 5 percent of the Northeast in drought and 7 percent of the region as abnormally dry. The wet weather helped increase reservoir levels, allowing water restrictions to be lifted in some locations. Record-low streamflow was found at times, particularly during the first half of the month, in the region's southeastern corner including southeastern Pennsylvania, southern New Jersey, northern Delaware, and eastern Maryland. Groundwater recovery generally lagged, with record low levels in places like central Maryland and parts of New Jersey.

##### Notable Weather

 During May, there were several rounds of severe weather and/or flash flooding, with the Mid-Atlantic being a focal point for many of the events: 
*   _May 1 to 6_  
 Severe weather and/or flash flooding occurred somewhere in the Northeast every day during this period. This included four weak (EF-0 or EF-1) tornadoes in central/eastern Pennsylvania and damaging straight-line winds of up to 85 mph in central New York. Large hailstones of 2.00 inches (lime sized) and 2.50 inches (tennis ball sized) were reported in central West Virginia and western Pennsylvania, respectively, with multiple reports of hail up to 1.75 inches (golf ball sized) across the Northeast. Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in some locations including eastern New York where rain totals generally topped out around 5 inches. Several storm-related injuries were reported in the region. 
*   _May 13 to 14_  
 Heavy rain in the Mid-Atlantic, between 2 and 5 inches in most areas, caused flash flooding. An area from West Virginia's Eastern Panhandle through western Maryland into south-central Pennsylvania was hit particularly hard, with rainfall amounts of up to 7 inches falling in just a few hours. There were numerous evacuations, water rescues, road closures, and buildings that took on water. A Flash Flood Emergency, signifying a dangerous, life-threatening situation, was issued by the National Weather Service for a portion of Allegany County in western Maryland, where students and staff from a school were evacuated by boat. Preliminary data shows that the nearby Georges Creek reached its second-highest level, with records back to the 1930s. A few other waterways in the hardest hit areas reached one of their 10 highest levels on record (which vary by location), as well. Flooding also occurred downstream of these areas, particularly along the Potomac River which was impacted by sewage overflows and buildup of debris. 
*   _May 16_  
 Four weak tornadoes touched down in the Mid-Atlantic, including one that caused damage in Baltimore, Maryland. This was part of a broader severe weather outbreak across the Mid-Atlantic that also featured damaging, non-tornadic winds and a few instances of large hail including a 2.50-inch (tennis ball-sized) hailstone in Baltimore County, Maryland. In addition, some areas saw localized flooding including portions of southeastern Pennsylvania where multiple water rescues were performed. 

For more information, please visit the [Northeast Regional Climate Center Home Page](http://www.nrcc.cornell.edu/).

#### Midwest Region _(Information provided by the [Midwest Regional Climate Center](https://mrcc.purdue.edu/))_

##### Temperature

The preliminary average May temperature for the Midwest was 59.1°F (15°C), which was 0.6°F (0.4°C) below the 1991-2020 normal. Temperature anomalies were 1 to 6°F (0.6 to 3.3°C) above normal across Minnesota, with temperatures closer to normal or slightly below normal across the region to the south and east. Preliminary statewide average temperatures ranged from 2.2°F (1.2°C) above normal for Minnesota to 1.7°F (0.9°C) below normal for Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio. Temperature departures oscillated from above normal to near normal to below normal for the first few weeks of May before widespread below-normal temperatures blanketed the region from May 22-31. Notably, record to near-record warmth stretched across the northwest portion of the region from May 11-15 as temperatures soared more than 25°F (13.9°C) above normal. Temperatures across northern Minnesota reached the mid- to upper-90s on May 11, followed by several more days with temperatures over 90°F (32.2°C). International Falls, Minnesota, reached 96°F (35.6°C) on May 11, setting an all-time high temperature record for the month and becoming the highest temperature ever measured that early in the calendar year. Southern Wisconsin reached its first 90°F (32.2°C) temperatures of the year on May 15, about a month ahead of normal. Meanwhile, locations across the lower Midwest, from southern Missouri eastward along and around the Ohio River, were void of reaching 90°F (32.2°C) during the month of May. The Midwest's preliminary average spring (March-May) temperature was 1.9°F (1.1°C) above normal. Preliminary rankings indicate that spring 2025 was tied for the 14th warmest on record for the Midwest.

##### Precipitation

Preliminary May precipitation totaled 3.84 inches (98 mm) for the Midwest, which was 0.54 inches (14 mm) below normal, or 88 percent of normal. Precipitation was near to above normal across the far lower Midwest, eastern Midwest, and central Minnesota. Elsewhere across the central and western Midwest, precipitation was 25 to 75 percent of normal. Preliminary statewide precipitation totals ranged from 2.22 inches (56 mm) above normal in Kentucky to 2.11 inches (54 mm) below normal in Iowa. Preliminary rankings indicate that Kentucky had its 8th wettest May on record. Several long-running stations in central and southeast Ohio had a top ten wettest May. Circleville, Ohio, had its 6th wettest May in 120 years, with 7.98 inches (202.7 mm) of rainfall. In western Kentucky, Mammoth Cave ended the month with 9.07 inches (230.4 mm), becoming the 8th wettest in 85 years of recordkeeping. In southwest Missouri, the town of Nevada logged its 5th wettest May in 114 years with 11.23 inches (285.2 mm). From northern Missouri northward to the Canadian border and northeastward into the western Great Lakes, much of the region had a 12-17 day stretch of consecutively dry weather in early May. Several long-running stations in Iowa achieved a top ten driest May. In southeast Iowa, Ottumwa measured 0.83 inches (21.1 mm) for May, the 2nd driest in 77 years of observations, and over 4 inches (101.6 mm) below normal for the month. Fayette, in northeast Iowa, had their 5th driest May in 130 years with just 1.39 inches (35.3 mm). Preliminary spring (March-May) precipitation for the Midwest totaled 11.47 inches (291.3 mm), which was 0.85 inches (21.6 mm) above normal. Preliminary rankings indicate that spring 2025 was the 23rd wettest on record for the Midwest.

##### Drought

During May, the lower Midwest remained free of abnormal dryness or drought. Scattered areas of abnormal dryness or drought lingered across the upper Midwest with little change from the start to the end of May. The one area of notable drought expansion during May was northern Illinois and northwest Indiana, which were blanketed with moderate (D1) drought by the end of the month.

##### Notable Weather

*   _Wildfires_  
 A prolonged stretch of warm, dry, and windy weather in early to mid-May created elevated wildfire risk across Minnesota and northern Wisconsin, with the most notable fire risk from May 11-14. In northeast Minnesota, three large fires ignited on May 12-13 and burned for weeks before full containment was achieved. Combined, these fires burned over 30,000 acres of land, destroying structures and forcing local evacuations. 
*   _May 15 Severe Weather Across the Upper Midwest_  
 A fast-moving, potent weather system brought tornadoes, damaging winds, and large hail to the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes on May 15. At least 31 tornadoes were confirmed across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Hail up to 3 inches (76.2 mm) in diameter fell along the southern Lake Michigan shore from Milwaukee throughout the Chicago area. Damaging winds gusting 50-80 mph (80.5-128.7 kph) were reported across a wide swath of the region, and a multi-county area in northwest Wisconsin had significant straight-line wind damage from winds that exceeded 100 mph (161 kph). 
*   _May 16 Severe Weather Across the Lower Midwest and Chicago Area Dust Storm_  
 A severe thunderstorm and deadly tornado outbreak initiated in eastern Missouri on May 16 and moved eastward across the lower Midwest, affecting Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, and Ohio. At least 16 tornadoes were confirmed across the multi-state area by the National Weather Service, including an EF-4 in southern Illinois with peak winds estimated at 190 mph (305.8 kph) and a long-track EF-4 in eastern Kentucky that caused 19 fatalities. An EF-3 tornado traversed a populated area of St. Louis, Missouri, killing four people and injuring dozens more while leaving an estimated $1 billion in storm damage to the city. Two other tornadoes in this outbreak caused a combined three additional deaths, bringing the human toll to at least 26 fatalities across the region. Additionally, very large hail (tennis ball to softball size) was reported in western Kentucky and central Indiana, and a wide stretch of 60-90 mph (96.6-144.8 kph) straight-line winds ripped across central and eastern Kentucky. As storms tracked across the lower Midwest, strong winds moved across dry farmland in northeast Illinois, kicking up a large dust storm that moved northeast into the Chicagoland area, northwest Indiana, and extreme southwest Michigan. The dust was driven by 60 mph (96.6 kph) winds, which resulted in very low visibility and crop damage. According to the National Weather Service, this area has not experienced a dust storm of this magnitude since the mid-1930s. 

For more information, please visit the [Midwest Climate Watch Home page](https://mrcc.purdue.edu/climate_watch.htm).

#### Southeast _(Information provided by the [Southeast Regional Climate Center](https://sercc.com/))_

##### Temperature

Temperatures were variable across the Southeast in May. Much of the interior of the region, as well as Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, were near to slightly below average, with some locations running 2 to 3°F (1.1 to 1.8°C) below average for the month. Temperatures were above average across the rest of the region, with many locations across Florida, southern Georgia, and the eastern Carolinas running 3 to 5°F (1.8 to 2.8°C) above average for the month. One year after experiencing their warmest May on record, Fort Lauderdale, FL (1912-2025), Fort Myers, FL (1902-2025), Tampa, FL (1890-2025), and West Palm Beach, FL (1888-2025) observed their second warmest May on record. Valdosta, GA (1948-2025) also recorded its second warmest May while Miami, FL (1895-2025) and Orlando, FL (1892-2025) tied their second warmest May on record, ranking just behind last year. Daytona Beach, FL (1923-2025), Key West, FL (1871-2025), and Punta Gorda, FL (1914-2025) tied their third warmest May on record. Tallahassee, FL (1896-2025) tied its fourth warmest May on record and Jacksonville, FL (1871-2025) recorded its fifth warmest May on record.

#### June Temperature

[![Image 6: June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202606.png) June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202606.png "June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) for the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) in June was 70.6°F, 2.2°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202606#1) of the 132-year record.

[Temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-tavg-202606.png) were above to much-above average across a large portion of the West, Southwest, the southern Plains, Florida, the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. The Southwest climate region tied its fifth-warmest June on record, averaging 4.9°F above its 20th-century baseline. Nine states experienced one of their 10 warmest Junes on record, with [New Mexico](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/29/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) and [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) each ranking third warmest. In contrast, below-average temperatures were observed across portions of the northern Rockies and Plains, while much of the Midwest and Southeast experienced near-average June conditions.

The CONUS [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) in June was 83.0°F, 1.7°F above average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmax/202606#1) of the 132-year record. The [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/1/6/1895-2026) was 58.3°F, 2.7°F above average, ranking as the [eighth-warmest June average nighttime temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmin/202606#1) on record.

Despite near- to below-average daytime highs across much of the South and Gulf Coast, nighttime minimum temperatures were elevated across these same areas. [Alabama's average maximum temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/1/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) was 2.0°F below the long-term average, while [Texas](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/41/tmin/1/6/1895-2026) tied its warmest June average minimum temperature on record at 71.9°F (4.4°F above average). Louisiana and New Mexico each recorded their second-warmest June minimum temperatures. Farther north, [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) recorded its warmest June average maximum temperature on record at 80.7°F (5.8°F above average), marking the first June since 1943 that the state's average daytime highs exceeded the 80°F threshold.

Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jun/1-month), temperature-related energy demand across the CONUS during June was 148 percent of average and the 22nd-highest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### June Precipitation

[![Image 16: June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202606.png) June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202606.png "June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The [total precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/1/6/1895-2026) averaged across the CONUS in June was 3.23 inches, 0.31 inch above the 20th-century average, ranking in the [wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/ranking/110/pcp) of the 132-year record.

Above-average precipitation was observed across portions of the far northern tier, central and southern Plains, South, Gulf Coast, Midwest and Great Lakes. In contrast, below-average precipitation was observed across parts of the West, Northwest, central and southern Rockies, as well as much of the Florida Peninsula, Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic region.

[Seven states](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/mapping/110/pcp/202606/1/pctavg)—Kansas, Oklahoma, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama—received precipitation totals more than 50 percent above their June average, while California, Nevada and Utah had precipitation deficits of at least 60 percent. Kansas, Illinois, Indiana and Kentucky each ranked among their 10 wettest Junes on record.

[Precipitation across Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/1/6/1925-2026) in June [ranked in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/50/pcp/202606#1) of the 102-year record. The state recorded 1.78 inches of precipitation, 0.56 inch below the 1925–2000 average. Below-average precipitation was observed across portions of the western and southern mainland, the Alaska Peninsula and Aleutians, and the Panhandle.

[Precipitation across Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/1/6/1895-2026) in June averaged 7.03 inches, 3.43 inches above the 1991–2020 average, [ranking as the second-wettest June](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/51/pcp/202606#1) in the 36-year record and the wettest since 1997. The wet conditions were associated with persistent strong trade winds during June, which enhanced orographic rainfall along windward slopes, especially on the Big Island.

#### Drought

According to the June 30 [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx) report, about 47.8% of the CONUS was in drought, a decrease of about 10.5% since the beginning of June. Drought persisted or intensified across much of the Northwest, Southwest, Great Basin and Rockies, as well as parts of the western Plains and the Mid-Atlantic from the Carolinas to the Northeast. Drought contracted or decreased in intensity across portions of the Plains, Midwest, lower Mississippi and Ohio Valleys, Southeast and far Northeast. Drought developed across portions of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

See the accompanying national [Drought Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/drought/202606) for further details.

#### Other Notable Events

Several notable events in June included:

*   **Central Gulf Coast:** The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur produced widespread flooding across the central Gulf Coast during June 16–19, with rainfall totals of 10 to 20 inches and a peak of 29.06 inches near Cottonport, Louisiana.
*   **Washington and Oregon:** A mid-June heat wave set numerous daily maximum temperature records across western portions of the Pacific Northwest, including a high of 97°F at Portland International Airport, Oregon, on June 15.
*   **Utah and Colorado:** Wildfires burned more than 120,000 acres across Utah and Colorado in late June. This included the 93,000-acre Cottonwood Fire in Utah and the lightning-ignited Knowles Fire that claimed the lives of three firefighters.
*   **Illinois and Indiana:** Record June tornado activity was observed across parts of the Midwest, with preliminary totals of 91 tornado reports in Illinois and 69 in Indiana. _See the [Tornadoes Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202606) for additional details._
*   **Delaware and Maryland:** On June 16, extreme drought (D3) expanded to cover about 65 percent of Delaware and 37 percent of Maryland, the greatest extent in both states since 2002.
*   **North Carolina and Virginia:** A mid-June heat wave produced triple-digit temperatures across parts of the Mid-Atlantic, including 104°F at Langley Air Force Base and John H. Kerr Dam in Virginia, and 103°F at Raleigh-Durham International Airport, North Carolina.
*   **South Dakota:** On June 29, a fast-moving mini-derecho tracked over 350 miles across South Dakota, producing a preliminary straight-line wind gust of 131 mph near Highmore and Holabird. _See the preliminary event summary ([NWS Aberdeen, SD](https://www.weather.gov/abr/June29thSignificantWindEvent))._
*   **Alaska:** Sitka, Alaska, reached 80°F on June 2, tying its third-highest temperature so early in the year. In contrast, Deadhorse recorded a low of 21°F on June 29—the station's lowest temperature during the June 15–September 8 period of record (since 1969).
*   **Puerto Rico:** Below-average June rainfall and above-average temperatures led to drought expanding to cover more than 40 percent of Puerto Rico.
*   **Hawaiʻi:** Strong trade winds across Hawaiʻi in June produced heavy rainfall along windward slopes, with Saddle Road Quarry on the Big Island recording a monthly total of 26.82 inches.

For additional details of notable June events please refer to the regional summaries below.

Much of the CONUS west of the Mississippi River experienced exceptionally warm conditions, with more than half of CONUS states ranking among their 10 warmest January–June periods on record. #### January–June Precipitation

[![Image 32: January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202606.png) January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202606.png "January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The average [precipitation total](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/ytd/6/1895-2026) across the CONUS during January–June was 13.65 inches, 1.65 inches below the 20th-century average, [ranking in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202606#6) of the 132-year record.

Year-to-date [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-prcp/grid-ranks-prcp-202601-202606.png) was below average across much of the West, Northwest, Great Basin, central and southern Rockies, and northern and north-central Plains. Much of the Southwest was also drier than average, from western Arizona through the Four Corners region into the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In contrast, portions of the southern border region from New Mexico into western and southern Texas received above-average precipitation, along with parts of the central Gulf Coast. Above-average January–June precipitation also extended across a broad region from the eastern south-central Plains through the middle Mississippi Valley into parts of the Upper Midwest, Great Lakes and interior portions of the Northeast. Remaining areas of below-average precipitation extended from Arkansas and northern Mississippi into the Tennessee Valley, lower Ohio Valley, and much of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.

Highlighting the contrast at the state level, [Michigan](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/20/pcp/6/6/1895-2026) recorded its wettest January–June on record, 6 inches above its long-term average, while Nevada, Arizona, Utah, Wyoming, and Colorado received only about half to two-thirds of their average precipitation for the six-month period. Along the East Coast, nine states from South Carolina to Massachusetts ranked among their eight-driest January–June periods on record. North Carolina and South Carolina each received less than two-thirds of their average total precipitation and, along with Virginia, experienced their driest January–June since 1986.

#### Extremes

The year-to-date [USCEI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/) was 129 percent above the long-term average, ranking as the second-highest January–June value in the 117-year record. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/1) spanned 78 percent of the CONUS, the second-largest extent on record, while warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/2) covered 66 percent of the CONUS, the third-largest extent on record. [Dry extremes](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/us/ytd/3), as measured by low Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) values, covered 46 percent of the CONUS—the largest January–June extent on record.

[Regionally](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/cei-hi), the Southwest set its highest January–June CEI value on record, while the West, South and Ohio Valley regions ranked second highest for the period. Warm extremes in [maximum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/1-hi) broke several January–June records, covering the entire West and Southwest regions (100 percent), along with 93 percent of the South (record high) and 97 percent of the Northwest (fourth highest). Warm extremes in [minimum temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/2-hi) were also widespread, spanning more than 98 percent of the West (record high), Southwest (record high) and South (second highest). The spatial extent of [very low PDSI](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/regional-overview/2026/ytd/3-lo) values set January–June records in the Southwest (96 percent) and Southeast (71 percent), and exceeded 40 percent across the West, Northwest, South, Ohio Valley and Northeast. In contrast, extreme 1-day precipitation totals set a January–June record in the [Ohio Valley](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/cei/graph/ce/ytd/4), covering more than 40 percent of the region.

#### Monthly Outlook

Above-average July [temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jun/usdotempoutlook-202606.gif) are favored across the West, South and East, with the greatest likelihood over the Northwest, southern Plains and Southeast. Above-average July [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jun/usdoprcpoutlook-202606.gif) is favored in the Great Basin and parts of the Southwest and Northeast, while below-average precipitation is favored for parts of the Pacific Northwest and western Gulf Coast.

[Drought](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jun/usdodroughtoutlook-202606.png) is expected to persist or expand across much of the Northwest and Rockies, as well as portions of the Plains, Mid-Atlantic and Puerto Rico, while drought improvement or removal is expected for parts of the Southwest and Southeast. Visit the [U.S. Monthly Drought Outlook](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/expert_assessment/mdo_summary.php) website for more details.

Significant wildland [fire potential for July](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/2026/jun/nifcfireoutlook-202606.png) is above normal across much of the Northwest, Great Basin and southern Rockies, as well as parts of the southern Plains, Carolinas, Florida Peninsula and Puerto Rico. For additional information on wildland fire potential, visit the [National Interagency Fire Center](https://www.nifc.gov/) website.

### Regional Highlights

These regional summaries were provided by the six [Regional Climate Centers](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/regional/regional-climate-centers) and reflect conditions in their respective regions. These six regions differ spatially from the [nine climatic regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/reference-maps/us-climate-regions) of the National Centers for Environmental Information.

#### Northeast _(Information provided by the [Northeast Regional Climate Center](http://www.nrcc.cornell.edu/))_

A hotter-than-normal June featured variable rainfall amounts and multiple rounds of severe weather that produced one of Pennsylvania's most active Junes for tornadoes.

**Read the full Northeast RCC report...**
##### **Temperature**

The average temperature for June in the Northeast was 66.5°F, which was 0.9°F hotter than normal. June average temperatures for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 0.2°F above normal in Pennsylvania and West Virginia to 2.7°F above normal in Rhode Island. This June ranked among the 20 hottest Junes since records began in 1895 for nine of the states: Rhode Island, third hottest; Delaware, seventh hottest; New Jersey, ninth hottest; Maryland, 11th hottest; Maine and Massachusetts, 12th hottest; New Hampshire, 13th hottest; Vermont, 16th hottest; and Connecticut, 17th hottest.

##### **Precipitation**

June precipitation in the Northeast totaled 3.81 inches, which was 86 percent of normal. Precipitation during June for the 12 Northeast states ranged from 51 percent of normal in Connecticut to 119 percent of normal in Vermont, with eight states being drier than normal.

##### **Drought**

The U.S. Drought Monitor from June 2 showed 34 percent of the Northeast in drought and 16 percent of the region as abnormally dry. During June, beneficial precipitation allowed drought and abnormal dryness to contract in the far ends of the Northeast: West Virginia and northern New England. For instance, by month's end, severe drought was removed from Maine and reduced to only small portions of southeastern New Hampshire and southern and eastern West Virginia, while moderate drought was confined to coastal Maine and contracted in New Hampshire and West Virginia. There were also improvements in a few spots in the Mid-Atlantic that saw locally heavy rainfall such as northern New Jersey, where moderate drought shrank in coverage. However, conditions deteriorated in some eastern portions of the Mid-Atlantic, southeastern New York, and southern New England. For example, extreme drought was introduced in southern and eastern Maryland, southern Delaware, and southeastern New Jersey, while severe drought was introduced in southeastern New York, southwestern Connecticut, and Rhode Island. As of June 9, 43.78 percent of Delaware was in extreme drought, its highest such coverage since August 27, 2002. The following week, as of June 16, 65.11 percent of Delaware was in extreme drought, its 10th-highest such coverage since the U.S. Drought Monitor began in 2000. At the same time, 36.96 percent of Maryland was in extreme drought, its high such coverage since August 27, 2002.

The U.S. Drought Monitor from June 30 showed 27 percent of the Northeast in drought and 11 percent of the region as abnormally dry. Drought conditions continued to have impacts in the region. During much of June, USGS 7-day streamflow and/or groundwater levels were record low along a path from Maryland to Massachusetts. Water conservation continued to be encouraged in some areas, with a few water suppliers in places like eastern Massachusetts having mandatory water restrictions or watering bans. A report from southwestern West Virginia noted that people continued to fill water tanks at the municipal water source. A well drilling company in eastern Maryland saw an uptick in business tied to drought conditions. Reports from West Virginia noted reduced water levels and hauling of water, germination and growth of some crops was limited, and hay yields in multiple locations were reduced by 50 percent to 80 percent compared to a typical year. Producers in that state reported that supplemental feed continued to be used for cattle due to poor pasture conditions, with some producers moving or selling off cattle earlier than usual due to poor pasture conditions and/or hay shortages. Growers in Delaware reported poor pasture conditions, impacts to hay growth, and irrigating crops earlier than usual which increased costs. Reports from eastern Maryland noted drought-stressed corn, delayed replanting of soybeans, and reduced honey production. In Massachusetts, some corn was slow to germinate and running behind schedule. With lawns turning brown due to warm, dry weather in Rhode Island, business for landscaping companies was impacted.

##### **Notable Weather**

 There were multiple rounds of severe weather in June. These storms produced a preliminary total of 29 tornadoes in the Northeast. This included 21 tornadoes in Pennsylvania, well above the state's June average of three tornadoes (based on data from 2001–2025) and qualifying it as one of the state's most active Junes for tornadoes since records began in 1950. Fayette County in Pennsylvania had four tornadoes, its greatest for any month on record. New York saw four tornadoes compared to its June average of one, with Lewis and Otsego counties seeing their first June tornadoes since 1987. Vermont and West Virginia each had two tornadoes, which was above average, with Windsor County, Vermont, having its first June tornado on record. Meanwhile, there were hundreds of wind damage reports across the region during June. Several of the severe weather events are highlighted below. 
*   June 6 — Six EF-1 tornadoes touched down in western Pennsylvania, with three having path lengths of over five miles. At their widest, two of the tornadoes were 400 yards (or just under a quarter mile). Damage from the tornadoes mostly consisted of snapped or uprooted trees. Thunderstorms also produced strong non-tornadic winds in the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern New York, with downed trees causing damage. “Top of the hour” wind gusts at the automated weather stations at LaGuardia Airport and Central Park in New York were among the highest such gusts for June at 64.4 mph and 53.0 mph, respectively. There were at least two deaths and at least 10 injuries tied to the storms. 
*   June 11–12 — Parts of the region experienced unusually hot temperatures and severe weather. Washington, D.C., and Islip, New York, tied their 10th-hottest temperatures for June of 100°F and 94°F, respectively. The heat caused some schools to close early. In addition, a few sites had one of their 10 warmest lows for June. Thunderstorm-related wind damage was reported across the region including downed trees and wires, damaged homes and vehicles, obstructed roads, and power outages. Some of the highest wind gusts included 69 mph at LaGuardia Airport, New York, and 67 mph at Dulles Airport, Virginia. Hailstones as large as 2.00–2.50 inches (lime to tennis ball sized) fell in Dutchess County, New York, qualifying as some of the largest hailstones reported in that county. There were at least two storm-related deaths. 
*   June 14 — There were 14 tornadoes in Pennsylvania, mostly in the northwestern quadrant of the state: one EF-2, eight EF-1s, and five EF-0s. It was among the greatest number of tornadoes on a June day in the state since records began in 1950 and likely among the 10 greatest such days for any month. Storm reports from the tornadoes noted damage to trees, roofs, siding, windows, etc. There were also many thunderstorm-related wind damage reports across the Mid-Atlantic including several concentrated areas of more intense damage. For instance, over 100 trees were damaged in a portion of Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, from estimated winds of up to 100 mph. Meanwhile, in Frederick County, Maryland, multiple structures like barns, houses, and a cell phone tower suffered significant damage from estimated wind speeds of up to 80 mph.

### June Highlights

#### June Temperature

[![Image 6: June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202606.png) June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202606.png "June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) for the contiguous U.S. (CONUS) in June was 70.6°F, 2.2°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202606#1) of the 132-year record.

[Temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-temp/grid-ranks-tavg-202606.png) were above to much-above average across a large portion of the West, Southwest, the southern Plains, Florida, the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. The Southwest climate region tied its fifth-warmest June on record, averaging 4.9°F above its 20th-century baseline. Nine states experienced one of their 10 warmest Junes on record, with [New Mexico](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/29/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) and [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) each ranking third warmest. In contrast, below-average temperatures were observed across portions of the northern Rockies and Plains, while much of the Midwest and Southeast experienced near-average June conditions.

The CONUS [maximum (daytime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) in June was 83.0°F, 1.7°F above average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmax/202606#1) of the 132-year record. The [minimum (nighttime) temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/1/6/1895-2026) was 58.3°F, 2.7°F above average, ranking as the [eighth-warmest June average nighttime temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tmin/202606#1) on record.

Despite near- to below-average daytime highs across much of the South and Gulf Coast, nighttime minimum temperatures were elevated across these same areas. [Alabama's average maximum temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/1/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) was 2.0°F below the long-term average, while [Texas](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/41/tmin/1/6/1895-2026) tied its warmest June average minimum temperature on record at 71.9°F (4.4°F above average). Louisiana and New Mexico each recorded their second-warmest June minimum temperatures. Farther north, [Rhode Island](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/37/tmax/1/6/1895-2026) recorded its warmest June average maximum temperature on record at 80.7°F (5.8°F above average), marking the first June since 1943 that the state's average daytime highs exceeded the 80°F threshold.

Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jun/1-month), temperature-related energy demand across the CONUS during June was 148 percent of average and the 22nd-highest value in the 132-year period of record.

The [average temperature for Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/tavg/1/6/1925-2026) in June was 50.5°F, 1.3°F above the 1925–2000 average, [ranking in the warmest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/50/tavg/202606#1) of the 102-year period of record. Above-average temperatures were primarily concentrated across southern portions of the Alaska mainland and the Panhandle region. The state's average maximum temperature was 59.6°F (1.5°F above average) and its average minimum temperature was 41.4°F (1.2°F above average); both ranked in the middle third of the historical record.

The [average temperature for Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/tavg/1/6/1895-2026) in June was 68.0°F, 0.3°F above the 1991–2020 average, [ranking in the middle third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/51/tavg/202606#1) of the 36-year record. Daytime maximum temperatures averaged 74.6°F (0.6°F below average), ranking in the coolest third of the record. The cooler daytime temperatures were offset by warm nighttime conditions, as minimum temperatures averaged 61.5°F (1.3°F above average), ranking as the third-warmest June average minimum temperature in the 36-year record.

#### June Precipitation

[![Image 16: June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202606.png) June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202606.png "June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The [total precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/1/6/1895-2026) averaged across the CONUS in June was 3.23 inches, 0.31 inch above the 20th-century average, ranking in the [wettest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/ranking/110/pcp) of the 132-year record.

Above-average precipitation was observed across portions of the far northern tier, central and southern Plains, South, Gulf Coast, Midwest and Great Lakes. In contrast, below-average precipitation was observed across parts of the West, Northwest, central and southern Rockies, as well as much of the Florida Peninsula, Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic region.

[Seven states](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/mapping/110/pcp/202606/1/pctavg)—Kansas, Oklahoma, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama—received precipitation totals more than 50 percent above their June average, while California, Nevada and Utah had precipitation deficits of at least 60 percent. Kansas, Illinois, Indiana and Kentucky each ranked among their 10 wettest Junes on record.

[Precipitation across Alaska](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/50/pcp/1/6/1925-2026) in June [ranked in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/50/pcp/202606#1) of the 102-year record. The state recorded 1.78 inches of precipitation, 0.56 inch below the 1925–2000 average. Below-average precipitation was observed across portions of the western and southern mainland, the Alaska Peninsula and Aleutians, and the Panhandle.

[Precipitation across Hawaiʻi](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/51/pcp/1/6/1895-2026) in June averaged 7.03 inches, 3.43 inches above the 1991–2020 average, [ranking as the second-wettest June](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/rankings/51/pcp/202606#1) in the 36-year record and the wettest since 1997. The wet conditions were associated with persistent strong trade winds during June, which enhanced orographic rainfall along windward slopes, especially on the Big Island.

#### Drought

According to the June 30 [U.S. Drought Monitor](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataTables.aspx) report, about 47.8% of the CONUS was in drought, a decrease of about 10.5% since the beginning of June. Drought persisted or intensified across much of the Northwest, Southwest, Great Basin and Rockies, as well as parts of the western Plains and the Mid-Atlantic from the Carolinas to the Northeast. Drought contracted or decreased in intensity across portions of the Plains, Midwest, lower Mississippi and Ohio Valleys, Southeast and far Northeast. Drought developed across portions of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

See the accompanying national [Drought Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/drought/202606) for further details.

#### Other Notable Events

Several notable events in June included:

*   **Central Gulf Coast:** The remnants of Tropical Storm Arthur produced widespread flooding across the central Gulf Coast during June 16–19, with rainfall totals of 10 to 20 inches and a peak of 29.06 inches near Cottonport, Louisiana.
*   **Washington and Oregon:** A mid-June heat wave set numerous daily maximum temperature records across western portions of the Pacific Northwest, including a high of 97°F at Portland International Airport, Oregon, on June 15.
*   **Utah and Colorado:** Wildfires burned more than 120,000 acres across Utah and Colorado in late June. This included the 93,000-acre Cottonwood Fire in Utah and the lightning-ignited Knowles Fire that claimed the lives of three firefighters.
*   **Illinois and Indiana:** Record June tornado activity was observed across parts of the Midwest, with preliminary totals of 91 tornado reports in Illinois and 69 in Indiana. _See the [Tornadoes Report](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sotc/tornadoes/202606) for additional details._
*   **Delaware and Maryland:** On June 16, extreme drought (D3) expanded to cover about 65 percent of Delaware and 37 percent of Maryland, the greatest extent in both states since 2002.
*   **North Carolina and Virginia:** A mid-June heat wave produced triple-digit temperatures across parts of the Mid-Atlantic, including 104°F at Langley Air Force Base and John H. Kerr Dam in Virginia, and 103°F at Raleigh-Durham International Airport, North Carolina.
*   **South Dakota:** On June 29, a fast-moving mini-derecho tracked over 350 miles across South Dakota, producing a preliminary straight-line wind gust of 131 mph near Highmore and Holabird. _See the preliminary event summary ([NWS Aberdeen, SD](https://www.weather.gov/abr/June29thSignificantWindEvent))._
*   **Alaska:** Sitka, Alaska, reached 80°F on June 2, tying its third-highest temperature so early in the year. In contrast, Deadhorse recorded a low of 21°F on June 29—the station's lowest temperature during the June 15–September 8 period of record (since 1969).
*   **Puerto Rico:** Below-average June rainfall and above-average temperatures led to drought expanding to cover more than 40 percent of Puerto Rico.
*   **Hawaiʻi:** Strong trade winds across Hawaiʻi in June produced heavy rainfall along windward slopes, with Saddle Road Quarry on the Big Island recording a monthly total of 26.82 inches.

For additional details of notable June events please refer to the regional summaries below.

#### January–June Temperature

[![Image 22: January–June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202606.png) January–June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidetavgrank/statewidetavgrank-202601-202606.png "January–June 2026 Statewide Temperature Ranks Map")

The year-to-date [average temperature](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tavg/ytd/6/1895-2026) for the CONUS during the January–June period was 51.9°F, 4.4°F above the 20th-century average, [ranking as the second-warmest](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/tavg/202606#6) January–June period in the 132-year record. Much of the CONUS west of the Mississippi River experienced exceptionally warm conditions, with more than half of CONUS states ranking among their 10 warmest January–June periods on record. Nine states set new records for their warmest January–June period on record.

Based on the [NOAA climate regions](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/mapping/-1/tavg/202606/ytd/rank), the West and Southwest each experienced their warmest January–June period on record, while the South ranked as second warmest. The [Southwest region](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/regional/time-series/107/tavg/ytd/6/1895-2026) was especially anomalous, averaging 6.2°F above its 20th-century January–June baseline and eclipsing the previous record, set in 2000, by 2.0°F.

Both the average [maximum (daytime)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmax/ytd/6/1895-2026) and [minimum (nighttime) temperatures](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/tmin/ytd/6/1895-2026) ranked as the second warmest on record for the January–June period. The average maximum temperature was 64.3°F, 5.0°F above the 20th-century average, while the average minimum temperature was 39.5°F, 3.8°F above average. Based on [NOAA's Residential Energy Demand Temperature Index (REDTI)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/redti/time-series/USA/jun/year-to-date), energy demand for the CONUS from January through June was 35 percent of average, ranking as the sixth-lowest value in the 132-year period of record.

#### January–June Precipitation

[![Image 32: January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202606.png) January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/statewidepcpnrank/statewidepcpnrank-202601-202606.png "January–June 2026 Statewide Precipitation Ranks Map")

The average [precipitation total](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/time-series/110/pcp/ytd/6/1895-2026) across the CONUS during January–June was 13.65 inches, 1.65 inches below the 20th-century average, [ranking in the driest third](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/national/rankings/110/pcp/202606#6) of the 132-year record.

Year-to-date [precipitation](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/monitoring-content/sotc/national/grid-ranks-prcp/grid-ranks-prcp-202601-202606.png) was below average across much of the West, Northwest, Great Basin, central and southern Rockies, and northern and north-central Plains. Much of the Southwest was also drier than average, from western Arizona through the Four Corners region into the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In contrast, portions of the southern border region from New Mexico into western and southern Texas received above-average precipitation, along with parts of the central Gulf Coast. Above-average January–June precipitation also extended across a broad region from the eastern south-central Plains through the middle Mississippi Valley into parts of the Upper Midwest, Great Lakes and interior portions of the Northeast. Remaining areas of below-average precipitation extended from Arkansas and northern Mississippi into the Tennessee Valley, lower Ohio Valley, and much of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.

Highlighting the contrast at the state level, [Michigan](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/climate-at-a-glance/statewide/time-series/20/pcp/6/6/1895-2026) recorded its wettest January–June on record, 6 inches above its long-term average, while Nevada, Arizona, Utah, Wyoming, and Colorado received only about half to two-thirds of their average precipitation for the six-month period. Along the East Coast, nine states from South Carolina to Massachusetts ranked among their eight-driest January–June periods on record. North Carolina and South Carolina each received less than two-thirds of their average total precipitation and, along with Virginia, experienced their driest January–June since 1986.
